The workload favors SWAR: inputs are std::to_string of uniformly random 64-bit values, so nearly all are 19-20 digits (two full 8-digit words), and short numbers are not measured. parse_u64 is not a drop-in strtoull: no whitespace skipping, sign, base prefix, locale or errno. Shared cloud VM: results/fastest.json's own caveat says absolute ns are not stable across runs, so only ratios within one row are meaningful.

corrections.workload: bench/bench_doing_less.cpp bench_binary_search(): 20,000 random-key lower_bound queries over sorted int arrays of 4096 ints (16 KiB, L1-resident) and 4,194,304 ints (16 MiB, exceeds L2). Compares a branchless-cmov lower_bound, a branchless+prefetch variant and an Eytzinger (breadth-first, with prefetch) layout against std::lower_bound; gcc 13.3.0 -O2 -march=native, min of 7 samples.
corrections.caveats: Developer source is a PRIVATE repo, readable only via authenticated `gh api`, so it is capped below tier A despite full compiler/flags/CPU disclosure in results/fastest.json. include/fastcpp/algo/binary_search.hpp documents the same cmov-vs-branch finding, and the win depends on exact source spelling: `cond ? base+half : base` compiles to a branch on gcc 13 and gains nothing. Only libstdc++/gcc was tested; no libc++ or MSVC STL run. First-party benchmark, not independently reproduced. The repo labels the DRAM row 'UNSTABLE ROW': plain branchless measured 0.72x-1.49x of std::lower_bound over five runs. binary_search.hpp's own comment records the prefetch variant as 'a stable 1.6x', against 1.91x in this row, so the DRAM ratio varies from run to run. Prefetch is a loss on the L1 array (14.877 vs 11.562ns). The Eytzinger-vs-std::lower_bound 5.34x is a cross-row derived ratio. Both rows share run 2026-09-02-core and the identical 4.2M-int workload, but the bench times Eytzinger separately and does not checksum it against std::lower_bound, because it returns a tree index. Eytzinger ties branchless on the 16 KiB array (11.387 vs 11.577ns), needs a build step, and leaves the array unsorted.

notes: All numbers (5.83x, 1.91x, 80.132ns, 3.96x vs 317.093ns, derived 5.34x) match results/fastest.json and the bench source. I only added the repo's own instability flags and the missing Eytzinger checksum validation to caveats, and made the workload precise (20k queries, n = 4,194,304).

corrections.caveats: Repo private:developer-source is PRIVATE and readable only via the authenticated gh CLI, so it is capped below tier A despite full compiler/flags/CPU disclosure. The 4-element workload is close to the best case for inline storage (well under the 8-slot inline capacity), and the results file has no row testing the crossover point where elements overflow to the heap. The baseline is not reserve()d: bench_small_vectors push_backs 4 ints into an empty std::vector<int>, which under libstdc++'s 1->2->4 growth costs 3 heap allocations and 2 relocations per vector, where small_vector does none. So the 21.34x measures malloc avoidance plus regrowth, not one allocation versus none; a reserve(4) or std::array/pmr baseline was not measured. Timings are ns per vector (ops_per_iteration = 50,000), min of 7 samples, on a shared cloud VM where absolute ns are not stable across runs.

notes: The 1.856 vs 39.6ns (21.34x) figure matches results/fastest.json and bench/bench_doing_less.cpp exactly. I added the un-reserved std::vector growth caveat (3 mallocs per baseline vector) and the run commit to compiler_and_flags; nothing else needed changing.
